blocks.md:
Almost every technical interview gets to this within ten minutes, because the bridge from **equity value** to **enterprise value** is a quick test of whether you understand *who owns what* in a company. If you can walk it confidently, with a number attached to each step, the interviewer relaxes and moves on to valuation. If you stumble, the rest of the interview turns into a rescue mission.

You only need one mental picture and one worked example. This lesson gives you both.

blocks.heading: One business, several people with a claim on it
blocks.md:
Imagine a company as a single machine that spits out cash every year. Several groups have a claim on that cash:

- **Shareholders** — they own the leftover after everyone else is paid.
- **Lenders** — they are owed interest and eventually their money back.
- **Preferred shareholders, minority owners, lease providers** — smaller groups who sit somewhere between the two.

**Equity value (EqV)** is what the *shareholders'* slice is worth: share price × diluted shares.

**Enterprise value (EV)** is what the *whole machine* is worth, regardless of who financed it. It is what a buyer would need to hand over to own the business outright and owe nobody.

The bridge is simply: start with the shareholders' slice, then add the other claims on top. The one twist is **cash**: a buyer effectively gets the company's cash back the moment they own it, so cash reduces the true price.

The bridge, written out:

$$\text{EV} = \text{EqV} + \text{Debt} - \text{Cash} + \text{Preferred} + \text{NCI} + \text{Lease liabilities}$$

Read each item as a question — *does this claim rank ahead of ordinary shareholders, and does a buyer have to deal with it?*

| Item | Add or subtract | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Debt (bonds, loans, overdrafts) | **+** | The buyer inherits it and must repay it |
| Cash & equivalents | **−** | The buyer can use it to pay down the debt they just inherited |
| Preferred shares | **+** | Paid before ordinary shareholders; behaves like debt |
| Non-controlling interest (NCI) | **+** | The consolidated numbers include 100 % of a subsidiary, so EV must reflect 100 % of it |
| Lease liabilities (IFRS 16) | **+** | Since 2019 leases sit on the balance sheet as a debt-like obligation; add them if your EBITDA excludes lease costs |

Two habits that stop mistakes:

1. **Use diluted shares** for EqV — options and convertibles that are in the money are shareholders-in-waiting.
2. **Net debt** is a shorthand for *debt − cash*. If someone gives you net debt, don't subtract cash a second time.

**Harbourline plc**, a UK logistics company. From its latest annual report and today's share price:

- Share price £4.20, diluted shares 250m
- Borrowings £500m, cash £120m
- Preferred shares £30m, non-controlling interest £25m, lease liabilities £45m

Build EV one line at a time:

One further item sits in the notes rather than on the face of the balance sheet: an **unfunded pension deficit of £35m**. It is a stretch item — see the final step.

**"Cash is an asset, so surely it makes the company worth more — why subtract it?"**

It does make the *shares* worth more: cash is already inside equity value, because the market price reflects it. The bridge is not saying cash is bad. It is saying that once you own the whole company, the cash is yours to use against the debt you have taken on, so the *net* amount you are really paying for the operating business is lower.

The second-most-common slip is the direction of NCI. Students subtract it because "we don't own that bit". But the point of EV is to match the *consolidated* EBITDA, which includes 100 % of the subsidiary. To make numerator and denominator consistent you **add** NCI.

One more slip to guard against: if an interviewer hands you *net debt* directly, that figure has already had cash taken out of it. Subtracting cash again is a double-count, and it is a surprisingly easy mistake to make under pressure when you are working through the bridge line by line.

Equity value is the value of the shares — price times diluted share count. Enterprise value is the value of the whole operating business to all capital providers. To get from one to the other you add the claims that rank ahead of ordinary shareholders — debt, preferred shares, non-controlling interests and lease liabilities — and subtract cash, because a buyer can use the company's own cash to pay down what it inherits. For Harbourline that is £1,050m of equity, plus £380m net debt, plus £100m of other claims, giving an EV of about £1.5bn.

blocks.prompt: Harbourline plc raises £100m of new debt and holds the cash on its balance sheet. What happens to its enterprise value?

options.label: It depends on the interest rate

blocks.explain_md: Debt goes up £100m, but so does cash — and the bridge *adds* debt and *subtracts* cash. The two moves cancel, so enterprise value does not budge. That is the point of EV: it measures the operating business, and borrowing money does not make the business better at what it does. Equity value is unchanged too, at least on day one. Drag the debt and cash sliders below together and watch the total sit still.

blocks.prompt: Harbourline uses £100m of its cash to repay £100m of its borrowings. What happens to equity value and enterprise value?

options.label: Equity value is unchanged, but enterprise value falls by £100m
Equity value falls by £100m, but enterprise value is unchanged

blocks.explain_md:
Cash drops from £120m to £20m and borrowings drop from £500m to £400m. Net debt was 500 − 120 = £380m; it is now 400 − 20 = **£380m**. Identical.

So enterprise value does not move. Neither does equity value: the company handed over an asset and extinguished a liability of exactly the same size, so the shareholders' stake is worth precisely what it was.

This is the mirror image of the earlier prediction. Raising debt and holding the cash left both values alone; spending cash to clear debt leaves both alone too. In each case the *composition* of the balance sheet changed while the **net** position did not — and the bridge only ever cared about the net position.

tmt.heading: The bridge lines that trip people up in tech
tmt.md:
The previous lesson covered why a cash-rich technology company can have an enterprise value below its market capitalisation. Here the question is narrower and more practical: which lines of the bridge behave differently, and what do you actually do with them?

Two come up constantly. **Convertible bonds** are debt that turns into shares if the price rises far enough, so they sit in exactly one of two places and never both. Deep in the money, treat them as equity: add the shares they would convert into and leave the principal out of the bridge. Out of the money, treat them as ordinary debt and leave the share count alone. Say which you are assuming *before* you compute anything — the interviewer is testing whether you noticed the choice existed.

The second is **share-based compensation**. It does not appear in the bridge at all, but it quietly inflates the share count every year, so a diluted count taken from last year's accounts understates today's equity value.
tmt.example_q: A software company has a £5bn market cap, £800m of cash, £200m of convertible debt trading well in the money, and no other debt. What is its enterprise value?
tmt.answer_md:
The convertible is deep in the money, so I would treat it as equity rather than debt: it will convert into shares, and I add those shares to the diluted count instead of adding £200m of debt.

On that basis enterprise value is the £5bn equity value — already including the converted shares — less £800m of cash, so about **£4.2bn**. If the convertible were out of the money I would instead leave the share count alone and add the £200m as debt, giving £4.4bn. The important part is stating the assumption before doing the arithmetic.

healthcare.heading: The bridge lines that trip people up in healthcare
healthcare.md:
The previous lesson covered why a cash-rich biotech can have a very small enterprise value. The practical question here is which claims belong in the bridge alongside ordinary borrowings.

The awkward one is **milestone and royalty obligations** owed to a partner or a licensor. They are not borrowings, and they are contingent — payable only if a drug hits a development or sales target. But they are contractual claims that rank ahead of shareholders, so many analysts add the present value of the committed portion as a debt-like item. There is no settled convention; what matters is that you name the item, say how you are treating it and why, and stay consistent across every company you compare.

**Convertible debt** is common here too, for the same reason it is common in software: pre-profit companies raise it because it is cheap. Treat it exactly as you would in tech — shares if it is in the money, debt if it is not.
healthcare.example_q: A biotech has a £400m market cap and £450m of cash after a raise. What does a negative enterprise value tell you?
healthcare.answer_md:
Enterprise value is roughly £400m less £450m, so about **negative £50m** — the market is valuing the operating business at less than nothing.

That is a statement about expected burn, not a free lunch. The market is saying it expects the company to spend that cash on programmes that will not generate a return, so a pound inside this company is worth less than a pound outside it. I would want to know the runway, what the next data readout is and when it lands, because that readout is what the whole valuation is really about.

blocks.prompt: Harbourline raises £100m of new debt and leaves the cash on its balance sheet. What happens to equity value and enterprise value?

is.note: No time has passed, so no interest has been charged yet

blocks.check: Equity value is unchanged (the shares are worth the same: the company has £100m more cash and £100m more debt). Enterprise value is also unchanged: +£100m debt and −£100m cash cancel in the bridge. Raising debt does not create value by itself — only what you *do* with the money does.

blocks.prompt:
**Marlow Foods** trades at £12.50 with 80m diluted shares. It has £260m of bonds, £340m of cash, no preferred shares, £15m of NCI and £20m of lease liabilities. Say the bridge out loud, then calculate its enterprise value. Is EV bigger or smaller than equity value, and why?

**Stretch:** the notes also disclose a **£25m unfunded pension deficit**. Does that change your answer?
blocks.model_answer_md:
Equity value = 12.50 × 80 = **£1,000m**.

Net debt = 260 − 340 = **−£80m** (net *cash*).

EV = 1,000 − 80 + 0 + 15 + 20 = **£955m**.

EV is *smaller* than equity value because Marlow has more cash than debt. A buyer would pay £1,000m for the shares, inherit £260m of bonds, but immediately get £340m of cash back, so the operating business really costs about £955m once the smaller claims are added.

**Stretch — the pension deficit.** A deficit is money Marlow must eventually put in from its own cash, so most analysts treat it exactly like debt and add it to the bridge:

EV = 955 + 25 = **£980m**.

The test is the one used for every other line: does this claim rank ahead of ordinary shareholders, and will a buyer have to deal with it? A funding shortfall on a pension scheme passes both, so it goes in. Say the assumption out loud — some analysts add it after tax, since the contributions are deductible.
rubric: Uses diluted shares to get £1,000m equity value
Computes net debt as negative (net cash of £80m)
Adds NCI and leases, arrives at ~£955m
Explains that net cash makes EV lower than EqV
Stretch: treats the pension deficit as debt-like and reaches ~£980m, stating the assumption

pairs.a: Yes in theory, when cash exceeds equity value plus all other claims — the market thinks the operating business destroys value. It is rare and usually a sign of distress or a mispricing.

pairs.q: Why use diluted rather than basic shares?
pairs.a: In-the-money options and convertibles will become shares if the company is bought, so a buyer must pay for them too.

pairs.q: A company pays a £50m dividend. EqV and EV?
pairs.a: Equity value falls by £50m (cash left the company). EV is unchanged: cash −50 means the bridge adds back £50m more net debt.

pairs.q: Which is bigger in the bridge, EV or EqV, for a typical FTSE 100 company?
pairs.a: EV — most large companies carry more debt than cash, so net debt is positive and gets added.

blocks.md: **Equity value is the shareholders' slice; enterprise value is the whole pie — add the other claims, subtract the cash.**

items: Explain in one breath why cash is subtracted and NCI is added
Bridge from share price to enterprise value for any listed company using its balance sheet
Say what a debt raise, a dividend or a cash acquisition does to EqV and EV
Spot the double-count when someone gives you net debt and cash separately
